title: Async JavaScript & Error Handling
intro: Almost every Node bug that reaches production is an async bug: a promise nobody awaited, an error thrown where no catch can see it, a loop that did not wait, or a fan-out that flattened a database. Interviewers use these questions to see whether you can predict what runs when and where an error goes. A senior answer explains the mechanism (promises, microtasks, the event loop), names the failure mode, and shows the production fix: limits, timeouts, cancellation, retries and a clear crash policy.

questions.title: Callbacks to Promises to async/await
questions.question: Walk me through how async code evolved in Node: callbacks, Promises, async/await. What is an error-first callback, what is callback hell, and how do you turn a callback API into a Promise API?
questions.short: Node started with error-first callbacks: the last argument is a function called as `cb(err, result)`, and you must check `err` first. Nesting many of them gives callback hell: deep indentation, error checks repeated at every level, and easy-to-miss bugs like calling the callback twice. Promises turned the result into a value you can return, chain and combine, with one `.catch` for the whole chain, and async/await is syntax on top of Promises that lets you write that chain like normal code with `try/catch`. To convert an old API I use `util.promisify`, or the built-in Promise versions like `fs/promises` and `timers/promises`.
questions.simple: A callback is "call me when you are done". A Promise is a receipt you can hold, pass around and wait on. async/await lets you wait on that receipt as if the code were normal step-by-step code.

explain.p: The Node convention: the callback is the last argument, and its first parameter is the error (or `null`). Success data comes after it. Every core callback API follows this, which is what makes generic tools like `util.promisify` possible.

explain.caption: Check err first, then return.

explain.p: When step 2 needs the result of step 1, you nest. Three or four steps later the code drifts right, each level repeats `if (err) return cb(err)`, and a `throw` inside a callback is not caught by any outer `try/catch`. Common bugs: forgetting to `return` after calling `cb(err)` (so the callback runs twice), or never calling it on one code path (so the caller hangs forever).

explain.caption: The "pyramid of doom".

explain.p: A Promise is an object that represents a future result. It is pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason, exactly once. Because it is a value, you can return it, store it, and combine many with `Promise.all`. One `.catch` at the end handles a failure anywhere in the chain.

explain.caption: Same flow, flat, with one error path.

list: `util.promisify(fn)` wraps any error-first function and returns a function that returns a Promise.
Prefer built-in Promise APIs when they exist: `node:fs/promises`, `node:timers/promises`, `node:stream/promises`, `node:dns/promises`.
Some functions have a custom promisified version via `util.promisify.custom` (for example `setTimeout`), which `promisify` uses automatically.
If you promisify a method, bind it first: `promisify(obj.method.bind(obj))`, otherwise `this` is lost.
The reverse exists too: `util.callbackify(asyncFn)` for code that still expects callbacks.

explain.note: async/await does not make code run in parallel or on another thread. It is still one thread and one event loop; it only changes how you write the waiting.

anim.title: util.promisify turns a callback into an awaitable Promise

steps.note: `readUser` is a classic error-first callback API: it calls `cb(err)` or `cb(null, data)` later.
`util.promisify` returns a new function. When called, it creates a Promise and passes a hidden `(err, value)` callback to `readUser`.
We call `main()`. It runs synchronously until its first `await`.
`readUserP(1)` starts a 10ms timer and returns a pending Promise. `await` pauses `main` and gives the thread back to the event loop.
The timer fires. The hidden callback gets `(null, user)` and resolves the Promise. Resuming `main` is queued as a microtask.
`main` resumes with the user object and logs it.
Second call with a bad id. Another timer starts and `main` waits again.
This time the callback gets an Error as its first argument, so the hidden callback REJECTS the Promise.
A rejected `await` throws at that line, so a normal `try/catch` catches it. No `if (err)` checks needed.

followups.q: How does util.promisify know which argument is the error?
followups.a: It assumes the Node convention: the callback is the last argument and is called as `(err, value)`. If `err` is truthy it rejects, otherwise it resolves with `value`. For APIs that break the convention you write a manual `new Promise` wrapper or provide `util.promisify.custom`.

followups.q: What happens if a callback API calls its callback twice?
followups.a: With callbacks, your code runs twice, which is a real bug source. A Promise can only settle once, so the second call is silently ignored. That hides the bug, so the API should still be fixed.

followups.q: Is async/await slower than callbacks?
followups.a: There is a small overhead per await (allocating promises, a microtask hop), but in modern V8 it is tiny compared to any real I/O. Readability and correct error handling matter far more for almost all backend code.

mistakes: Forgetting to `return` after `cb(err)`, so the success path also runs.
Wrapping a callback in `new Promise` and throwing inside the async callback, which is not caught by the Promise constructor.
Promisifying a method without binding it, so `this` is undefined.
Thinking async/await makes code multi-threaded.

questions.title: Promise states and chaining
questions.question: What states can a Promise be in? What does `.then` return, and what happens if you forget to `return` inside a `.then`? What does an async function return?
questions.short: A Promise is pending, then settles once: fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. `.then` always returns a NEW promise, resolved with whatever the handler returns; if the handler returns a promise, the new one follows it, and if it throws, the new one rejects. If you forget `return`, the next step gets `undefined` and does not wait for the inner work. An async function always returns a Promise: returned values fulfil it and thrown errors reject it.
questions.simple: Each `.then` is a new step on a conveyor belt. Whatever you put back on the belt with `return` goes to the next step. Put nothing back and the next step gets an empty box.

explain.p: "Resolved" is not the same as "fulfilled". A promise resolved with another promise is locked to it and is still pending until that one settles.

list: Handler returns a plain value: the new promise fulfils with it.
Handler returns a promise or thenable: the new promise waits for it and copies its outcome.
Handler throws: the new promise rejects with the thrown error.
Handler returns nothing: the new promise fulfils with `undefined`, immediately, without waiting for anything you started inside.

explain.h: Async functions always return a Promise

explain.p: `async function f() { return 5 }` returns `Promise<5>`, not `5`. A `throw` inside becomes a rejection, even if it happens before the first `await`. That means callers must `await` or `.then` the result, and a `try/catch` around a call without `await` will not catch the error.

explain.note: Handlers passed to `.then` always run asynchronously as microtasks, even if the promise is already fulfilled. This makes timing predictable: code after `.then(...)` always runs first.

anim.title: Return vs no return inside .then

steps.note: `p` is already fulfilled with 1.
Attaching `.then` to a settled promise does not run the handler now. It is queued as a microtask. `.then` returns a new pending promise.
A second, independent chain on the same `p`. Its first handler is queued too.
`f()` is async, so it returns a Promise. Returning 5 fulfils it right away.
Proof: `r` is a Promise, not the number 5.
`r.then` queues its handler behind the other two.
Sync code is done, microtasks run. h1 computes 2 but returns nothing, so chainA fulfils with `undefined`. Its next handler is queued.
h2 RETURNS 2, so chainB fulfils with 2. Its next handler is queued.
The handler on `r` runs and receives 5.
Chain A gets `undefined` because the previous handler had no `return`.
Chain B gets 2. The only difference was the `return`.

followups.q: What is the difference between .then(onOk, onErr) and .then(onOk).catch(onErr)?
followups.a: With the two-argument form, `onErr` does not catch errors thrown inside `onOk`, because they are on the same step. With `.then(onOk).catch(onErr)`, the catch is one step later, so it catches errors from `onOk` too.

followups.q: What does .finally receive and return?
followups.a: `.finally` gets no arguments and passes the original value or error through unchanged. The exception: if the finally handler throws or returns a rejected promise, that new error replaces the original outcome.

followups.q: Can a promise be resolved with another promise?
followups.a: Yes. It then adopts the other promise state. A promise can never be fulfilled with a thenable as its value; it always unwraps it.

mistakes: Using curly braces in an arrow function inside `.then` and forgetting `return`.
Calling an async function without `await` inside `try/catch` and expecting it to catch the error.
Saying "resolved" when they mean "fulfilled".
Thinking `.then` on an already fulfilled promise runs synchronously.

questions.title: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any
questions.question: Explain Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race and Promise.any. How does each behave when one input rejects, and when would you use each?
questions.short: `Promise.all` fulfils with all values in input order, but rejects as soon as any one rejects. `allSettled` never rejects; it waits for every input and gives you `{status, value | reason}` for each. `race` settles like the first input to settle, success or failure. `any` fulfils with the first success and only rejects, with an `AggregateError`, if all inputs reject. None of them cancel the losers; the other operations keep running.
questions.simple: `all`: everyone must pass. `allSettled`: give me everyone's report card. `race`: whoever finishes first, good or bad. `any`: the first one who passes.

head: Method
Fulfils when
Rejects when
Typical use
rows: All fulfil (array of values, input order)
Load several things you all need
Batch jobs, report which ones failed
First to settle is a success
First to settle is a failure
Fastest of several mirrors or replicas

explain.p: When `Promise.all` rejects early, the other promises still run to completion. Their results are ignored, and their later rejections are handled internally by `Promise.all`, so they do not trigger `unhandledRejection`. If those operations are expensive, pass an `AbortSignal` so you can actually stop them.

explain.caption: Pair Promise.all with an AbortController when losers should stop.

list: An empty array: `all` and `allSettled` fulfil with `[]`, `any` rejects with `AggregateError`, `race` stays pending forever.
Non-promise values in the array are treated like already-fulfilled promises.
`Promise.any` rejection: `err.errors` holds every individual reason.

explain.note: `Promise.all` on 10,000 items starts all 10,000 at once. It is a way to WAIT for many things, not a way to limit how many run. For limits see the concurrency question.

anim.title: Same inputs, four combinators

steps.note: Each combinator gets its own pair: one success after 50ms, one failure after 10ms. Both timers start immediately.
Same for allSettled.
And race and any. Eight timers in total; nothing has settled yet.
At 10ms the first failure fires. `Promise.all` short-circuits and rejects at once. Its 50ms input keeps running anyway.
allSettled records the failure and keeps waiting. It never short-circuits.
race settles like the FIRST input to settle. That was a failure, so race rejects.
any ignores failures while a success is still possible.
At 50ms the successes arrive. all and race are already settled and ignore them. allSettled now has both results.
any fulfils with the first success. It would only reject (AggregateError) if every input failed.

followups.q: If Promise.all rejects, do the other promises cause unhandled rejections when they fail later?
followups.a: No. `Promise.all` attached handlers to every input, so later rejections count as handled. They are just ignored.

followups.q: How would you build a timeout with these?
followups.a: Classic: `Promise.race([work, timeoutPromise])`. But that only stops waiting; the work keeps running and the timer keeps the process busy unless cleared. In modern Node, pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` to the operation so it is really cancelled.

followups.q: Does Promise.all keep the order of results?
followups.a: Yes, results are in input order, not completion order.

mistakes: Believing `Promise.all` cancels the other operations when one fails.
Using `Promise.all` for a batch where partial failure is fine, then losing all successful results on one error.
Confusing `race` (first to settle) with `any` (first to succeed).
Using `Promise.all` to "limit" work on huge arrays.

questions.title: Sequential vs parallel awaits
questions.question: You have two independent async calls. What is the difference between awaiting them one after the other and using Promise.all? When is sequential the right choice?
questions.short: Each `await` pauses the function until that promise settles, so `await a(); await b();` takes roughly a plus b. If the calls are independent, start both first and then wait for both with `Promise.all`, which takes roughly the slower of the two. Sequential is right when step 2 depends on step 1, when order matters, or when you must not overload a downstream service; for large lists you usually want something in between, a concurrency limit.
questions.simple: Sequential is boiling the kettle and only then starting the toast. Parallel is pressing both buttons, then waiting for both.

explain.p: Promises start their work when they are CREATED, not when they are awaited. `Promise.all` does not "run" anything; it only waits. The parallelism comes from calling both functions before the first `await`.

If `configP` rejects before you reach `await configP`, nothing is listening yet, and Node may treat it as an unhandled rejection and crash. `Promise.all` attaches handlers to both at once, so prefer it.

list: Data dependency: you need `user.id` to fetch orders.
Ordering matters: database migrations, writing log lines in order.
Protecting a downstream: a rate-limited API or a small DB pool. Use a concurrency limit rather than full parallel.
Transactions: queries on the same DB transaction/connection must be sequential anyway.

explain.note: In a loop, `for (const x of items) await work(x)` is intentionally sequential. `await Promise.all(items.map(work))` is fully parallel. Choose on purpose.

anim.title: for...of with await vs Promise.all

steps.note: First, the sequential version.
Task A starts. `await` pauses the loop, so B is not even created yet.
After 50ms A finishes. Only now does the loop move on.
B starts after A, even though B does not need anything from A.
B finishes. Total about 50 + 10 = 60ms.
Now the parallel version.
Both `task(...)` calls run while building the array, so C and D start together. Then `await` waits for both.
D is shorter and finishes first. Promise.all still waits for C.
C finishes at about 50ms. Total is the slowest task, not the sum.
Promise.all fulfils (results in input order: C, D) and `main` continues.

followups.q: Does Promise.all make CPU work faster?
followups.a: No. It only overlaps waiting. Two CPU-heavy synchronous functions still run one after the other on the main thread. For CPU parallelism you need worker threads or more processes.

followups.q: Is it safe to run many queries in parallel on one database transaction?
followups.a: Usually no. A transaction lives on one connection, and drivers queue or reject concurrent queries on it. Run them sequentially inside the transaction.

mistakes: Writing independent awaits one after another in a hot request path and doubling latency.
Believing `Promise.all` is what starts the work.
Starting promises early and awaiting them later one by one, risking unhandled rejections.
Going fully parallel over thousands of items and overwhelming a DB or API.

questions.title: The forEach + async pitfall
questions.question: What is wrong with `items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); })`? How do you fix it?
questions.short: `forEach` ignores the return value of its callback, so the promises returned by the async callback are thrown away. The loop does not wait, the code after it runs before any save finishes, all saves run in parallel with no limit, and any rejection becomes an unhandled rejection that can crash the process. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(...))` for parallel work, or a concurrency limiter for large lists.
questions.simple: `forEach` is a manager who hands out tasks and walks away without asking for any reports. `for...of` with `await` waits for each report before giving the next task.

explain.p: `Array.prototype.forEach` (and `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some`) are synchronous. They call your function and move on. An async function returns a Promise immediately, so `forEach` sees the promise, ignores it, and finishes. Nobody awaits those promises and nobody catches their errors.

list: `filter` with an async predicate is also wrong: every promise is truthy, so nothing is filtered.
`reduce` with async works only if you `await` the accumulator each step, and it is then sequential.
Node 22 also has `Array.fromAsync`, which collects an async iterable into an array, waiting for each item.

explain.note: Linters catch this: `@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises` and `no-floating-promises`. Turn them on in any Node codebase.

anim.title: forEach does not wait, for...of does

steps.note: `forEach` calls the async callback for 30. It runs to `await wait(30)`, starts a timer and returns a promise that forEach throws away.
Same for 10. forEach does not wait between items.
forEach is done. Nothing has finished, but the code after it runs anyway.
The for...of loop awaits `wait(60)`. This time `main` itself pauses.
At 10ms the forEach item 10 finishes. Note: shorter items finish first, so forEach order is not preserved.
At 30ms item 30 finishes, long after "after forEach" was printed.
At 60ms the first for...of item finishes. Only now does the loop start the next one.
The 20ms item finishes at about 80ms. Order is kept, one at a time.
With for...of, "after" really means after all items.

followups.q: What if one of the forEach callbacks throws?
followups.a: The async callback returns a rejected promise that nobody handles. Since Node 15 the default is to raise it as an uncaught exception, which crashes the process.

followups.q: Is `for await (const x of array)` the same as for...of with await?
followups.a: Not quite. `for await` over an array of promises awaits each element in order, but all promises were already created and running. It is parallel work consumed in order, and a later rejection can surface as unhandled before the loop reaches it.

mistakes: Using `forEach`, `map` without `Promise.all`, or `filter` with async callbacks.
Assuming the code after `forEach` runs after all items are processed.
Switching to `Promise.all(items.map(...))` on a huge array without thinking about load.

questions.title: Limiting concurrency
questions.question: You need to call an API for 10,000 IDs but only 5 requests may be in flight at a time. How do you implement that without a library?
questions.short: I use a worker-pool pattern: start N async "workers", each one loops, takes the next index from a shared counter, awaits the job, stores the result at that index, and repeats until the list is empty. `Promise.all` over the N workers resolves when everything is done. Because JavaScript is single-threaded, `next++` is safe without locks, and results stay in input order. In production I would also add error policy (fail fast or collect), cancellation, and maybe retries, or use a small library like `p-limit`.
questions.simple: Five checkout counters, one queue of customers. When a counter frees up, the next customer in line goes to it.

explain.p: `Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` starts all 10,000 requests immediately. You can exhaust sockets, file descriptors, DB pool slots, memory, or hit the remote rate limit. Chunking into batches of 5 is better, but each batch waits for its slowest item, so slots sit idle. A pool keeps exactly N busy at all times.
Sometimes tasks arrive over time rather than as a list. Then you want a function that wraps each call and queues it when the limit is reached.

list: Error policy: fail fast (as above), or wrap `fn` in try/catch and store `{ ok, value | error }` per item.
Cancellation: pass an `AbortSignal` and check `signal.aborted` in the worker loop.
Memory: for millions of items, read input as a stream or async iterator instead of holding one big array.
`queue.shift()` is O(n); for very large queues use an index or a linked list.

explain.note: Streams already do this: `stream.Readable.prototype.map(fn, { concurrency: 5 })` (experimental in Node 20/22) processes stream items with a concurrency limit.

anim.title: mapLimit with 2 workers

steps.note: Four jobs (their numbers are durations in ms), at most 2 at a time.
Two workers start. Worker 1 takes index 0 (60ms). It awaits, so worker 2 gets to run.
Worker 2 takes index 1 (10ms). Two jobs in flight: the limit is reached.
At 10ms the short job ends. Worker 2 stores 20 in results[1] and loops.
Worker 2 immediately takes index 2. No slot stays idle, unlike fixed batches.
At about 30ms the 20ms job ends.
Worker 2 takes the last item, index 3.
At 60ms worker 1 finishes, finds `next === length`, and exits its loop.
At about 130ms the last job ends and worker 2 exits too.
Both workers done, so Promise.all fulfils. Results are in INPUT order because each worker wrote to its own index.

followups.q: Why is `next++` safe with no lock?
followups.a: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time on the main thread. Between reading and incrementing `next` there is no `await`, so no other worker can run in between.

followups.q: How is this different from chunking into batches of 5?
followups.a: Batches wait for the slowest item in each batch before starting the next batch, so slots sit idle. A pool refills a slot as soon as it frees up, so throughput is higher.

followups.q: How would you collect errors instead of failing fast?
followups.a: Wrap the call in try/catch inside the worker and store `{ status: "rejected", reason }` at that index, like `allSettled` does, then decide after all items finish.

mistakes: Using `Promise.all` on the whole list and calling it "parallel processing".
Fixed batches with `Promise.all` per batch and assuming that is optimal.
Pushing results in completion order and losing the mapping to inputs.
Forgetting that the DB pool size is the real limit and setting concurrency far above it.

questions.title: Where errors go in async code
questions.question: How do you handle errors with async/await and with plain Promises? Why does a try/catch around setTimeout not catch an error thrown inside it?
questions.short: With async/await, a rejected promise makes `await` throw, so `try/catch` works, as long as you actually `await` inside the `try`. With plain Promises you use `.catch` at the end of the chain. `try/catch` only catches errors thrown while its block is on the call stack; a `setTimeout` or event callback runs later, from the event loop, after the `try` block has finished, so its error is uncaught. You must handle errors inside the callback, or turn it into a promise so the error flows to an `await`.
questions.simple: `try/catch` is a safety net under the code that is running right now. A timer callback jumps later, when the net has already been taken down.

head: Where the error happens
How you catch it
rows: Thrown inside a timer or raw callback
Nothing outside can; handle it inside

explain.h: return vs return await inside try

explain.p: Outside a `try` block, `return await` is not needed, but it does give better async stack traces. Inside a `try`, it is required for the `catch` to work.

explain.h: Throwing inside a Promise executor vs inside a callback

list: Throwing inside a `.then` handler or an async function is fine: it becomes a rejection.
Express 4 does not catch rejected promises from route handlers; you must call `next(err)` or use a wrapper. Express 5 forwards rejected promises to error middleware.
For EventEmitters, an `error` event with no listener is thrown, which usually crashes the process.

anim.title: Which catch catches what

steps.note: A last-resort listener so this demo can show what escapes. Real apps log and exit here.
`load()` throws, but because it is async, the throw becomes a rejected promise. `await` pauses `main`.
`main` resumes and the rejection is thrown at the `await` line, inside the `try`. The catch handles it.
Second style: no await, a `.catch` on the chain. The handler is queued because the promise is already rejected.
`setTimeout` only registers a callback. Registering cannot fail, so the `try` block finishes without error.
`main` continues synchronously in the same microtask.
The microtask queue is drained: the `.catch` handler runs.
At 10ms the timer callback throws. Its call stack starts at the event loop; the old `try` is long gone. It becomes an uncaught exception.
Only the process-level handler sees it. Without that handler, Node would print the stack and exit with code 1.

followups.q: How do you catch errors from a setTimeout callback properly?
followups.a: Use the promise version, `await setTimeout(ms)` from `node:timers/promises`, and then do the work after the await so errors flow to your try/catch. Or put try/catch inside the callback.

followups.q: Does an async Express 4 handler that throws send a 500?
followups.a: No. Express 4 ignores the returned promise, so the rejection is unhandled and the request hangs. Wrap handlers to call `next(err)` or upgrade to Express 5, which forwards rejections to error middleware.

mistakes: `return promise` inside a `try` and expecting the `catch` to handle its rejection.
Wrapping `setTimeout`, `emitter.on` or `fs.readFile` in try/catch to catch callback errors.
Throwing inside a callback inside `new Promise` instead of calling `reject`.
Catching an error, logging it, and silently continuing with bad state.

questions.title: unhandledRejection and uncaughtException
questions.question: What happens in Node when a promise rejection is not handled, or an exception is not caught? Should the process keep running after an uncaughtException?
questions.short: Since Node 15 the default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` mode raises an unhandled rejection as an uncaught exception, so the process crashes with exit code 1 unless you have an `unhandledRejection` listener. An uncaught exception also crashes the process by default. You can listen to `process.on("uncaughtException")`, but the official guidance is to use it only to log and clean up, then exit, because the app may be in an unknown state: half-done writes, leaked locks, broken invariants. Let a process manager such as Kubernetes or systemd restart it.
questions.simple: An uncaught exception is like a pilot finding an unknown warning light. You do not keep flying normally; you write down what happened and land the plane.

list: Uncaught exception: Node prints the error and stack and exits with code 1.
Unhandled rejection, no `unhandledRejection` listener: treated as an uncaught exception, so the process crashes the same way.
Unhandled rejection WITH a listener: the listener is called and the process does not crash. You own the decision.
Modes via `--unhandled-rejections`: `throw` (default), `strict`, `warn`, `warn-with-error-code`, `none`.

explain.p: "Unhandled" means: after the current microtask queue drains, the rejected promise still has no handler. If a handler is attached later, Node emits `rejectionHandled`.

An uncaught exception means a code path you did not plan for. It may have stopped halfway through updating shared state, left a DB transaction open, held a mutex, or not released a pool connection. Continuing can turn one crash into wrong data or a slow leak. Crashing loudly and restarting a clean process is safer, and with several instances behind a load balancer users barely notice.

head: Event
Fires when
Use it to
rows: A throw reaches the event loop
A rejected promise has no handler after a tick
Before uncaughtException; does not change behaviour
Process is about to exit (sync only)

explain.note: Domains (`node:domain`) were the old attempt to recover from uncaught errors. They are deprecated. Do not suggest them.

anim.title: Process-level safety nets

steps.note: Registering a listener for unhandledRejection changes the default: Node will call it instead of crashing.
Same for uncaught exceptions. `origin` tells you if it came from a throw or a rejection.
A promise is rejected and nobody attaches `.catch`. Node notes it as a candidate, but waits: a handler might still be added in this tick.
A timer that will throw is registered.
Main script finishes.
After the microtask queue drains, the rejection still has no handler. Node emits `unhandledRejection`.
Our listener runs. Without it, Node 15+ would crash here with exit code 1.
At 10ms the timer throws. No try/catch can be on the stack, so it reaches the event loop.
The listener runs and the process keeps going. That is dangerous in a real app: log, clean up, and exit.

followups.q: Is it ever OK to keep running after uncaughtException?
followups.a: Only if you are certain the error left no corrupted state, which is rarely provable. The Node docs say it is not safe to resume normal operation. Log, close resources, and exit; let a supervisor restart.

followups.q: What is the origin argument?
followups.a: It is `'uncaughtException'` for a normal throw, or `'unhandledRejection'` when the error came from an unhandled rejection in `throw` mode.

followups.q: How do you find who created an unhandled rejection?
followups.a: Use `Error` objects (not strings) as rejection reasons so you get a stack. Async stack traces in V8 help when the code uses `await`. Lint for floating promises to prevent it.

mistakes: Adding an `uncaughtException` handler that only logs and keeps serving traffic.
Thinking unhandled rejections are just warnings (that was before Node 15).
Rejecting with strings instead of Error objects, losing stack traces.
Calling `process.exit()` immediately, dropping in-flight requests and unflushed logs.

questions.title: Floating promises and fire-and-forget
questions.question: What is a floating promise? When is fire-and-forget acceptable, and how do you do it safely?
questions.short: A floating promise is one you create and never await, return, or attach `.catch` to. Its errors become unhandled rejections, which crash the process by default, and nothing waits for it, so it can still be running when you respond, shut down, or close a DB connection. Fire-and-forget is fine for non-critical side work like metrics or a best-effort cache refresh, but it must always have a `.catch`, should be tracked so shutdown can wait for it, and real must-not-lose work belongs in a durable queue, not an in-memory promise.
questions.simple: Sending a letter without a return address. If it fails, nobody ever finds out, or the post office (Node) panics.

list: Rejections are unhandled: process crash (Node 15+ default).
No ordering: the response is sent before the work finishes; a following request may read stale data.
Shutdown loses work: you close the DB pool while the promise still needs it.
In serverless (Lambda), the runtime can freeze after the response, so background work may never finish.
Tests become flaky: the test ends while work is still running.

explain.caption: Always catch, and keep track so shutdown can wait.

explain.p: If the work matters (sending the welcome email, charging a card), do not do it in memory. Write a job to a durable queue or an outbox table in the same DB transaction and let a worker process it with retries.

In TypeScript projects, enable `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` and `no-misused-promises`. When you really mean fire-and-forget, mark it with `void doThing().catch(log)` so the intent is visible.

explain.note: `void promise` alone silences the linter but not the crash. You still need `.catch`.

anim.title: A floating promise vs a caught one

steps.note: For the demo we log unhandled rejections. Without this listener, the first failure below would crash the process.
`signup` starts sending an email but does not await, return, or catch it. The promise floats.
The user is told everything is fine, even though the email has not been sent.
`signupSafe` also does not wait, but it attaches `.catch`, so any failure has a home.
Both functions finish immediately.
At 10ms Ann's email fails. Nobody is listening for that promise.
Node emits `unhandledRejection`. In a real app with default settings, the whole server would now exit.
At 50ms Bob's email fails too, but the `.catch` handles it: logged, no crash.

followups.q: Why not just await everything?
followups.a: Sometimes latency matters more than the side effect, for example analytics. Awaiting would slow the response for something the user does not need. Then fire-and-forget is reasonable, with a catch and tracking.

followups.q: How do you make sure background work finishes on shutdown?
followups.a: Track in-flight promises in a Set, and on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, then `await Promise.allSettled(inFlight)` with a timeout before closing DB pools and exiting.

mistakes: Calling an async function without await and without `.catch` inside a request handler.
Using `void` to silence the linter without adding error handling.
Doing must-not-lose work (payments, emails) as in-memory fire-and-forget.
Closing DB connections on shutdown while background promises still use them.

questions.title: Timeouts and cancellation
questions.question: How do you put a timeout on an async operation in Node, and how do you cancel it? Why is Promise.race with a timer not enough?
questions.short: Promises themselves cannot be cancelled, so Node uses `AbortController` and `AbortSignal`: you pass a signal into the operation and it stops its own work when the signal aborts. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives a signal that aborts by itself, and `AbortSignal.any([...])` combines a user cancel with a timeout. Many core APIs accept `{ signal }`: `fetch`, `fs.readFile`, `timers/promises` `setTimeout`, `events.once`, `stream.pipeline`, child processes. `Promise.race` with a timer only stops you waiting; the real work keeps running and holding resources.
questions.simple: Promise.race is hanging up the phone while the other person keeps talking. An AbortSignal is telling them "stop, I no longer need this".

list: `new AbortController()` gives you `.signal` and `.abort(reason)`.
`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts with a `TimeoutError` DOMException after `ms`. Its timer does not keep the process alive.
`AbortSignal.any([s1, s2])` aborts when any of them aborts (Node 20+).
`signal.aborted`, `signal.reason`, `signal.throwIfAborted()`, and the `abort` event.
APIs that support it usually reject with an `AbortError` whose `cause` is `signal.reason`.

explain.p: If you must use race (the API has no signal), clear the timer in `finally` and accept that the underlying work continues. For DB queries use the driver or server-side timeout (`statement_timeout` in Postgres).

Combine a per-request controller with client disconnect: abort when `req` closes early so you stop doing work for a client that is gone. Also know the built-in `server.requestTimeout` and `server.headersTimeout` settings on `http.Server`.

explain.note: Abort is cooperative. A signal does nothing unless the code you call checks it. A long synchronous loop cannot be interrupted at all.

anim.title: AbortSignal.timeout and AbortController

steps.note: Case 1: the job needs 100ms but the signal times out after 20ms.
At 20ms the signal aborts with a TimeoutError. The sleep listens to it, clears its own timer, and rejects right away.
The error is an AbortError, and its `cause` is the signal reason. The 100ms timer is gone, nothing is wasted.
Case 2: manual cancellation. Something else (a user, a shutdown) calls `abort()` after 10ms.
The job starts with the controller's signal.
At 10ms `abort()` fires, the sleep stops, and we catch an AbortError.
Case 3: a generous 500ms limit. The job starts.
The job finishes in 100ms, well within the limit. The timeout signal timer is unref'd, so it does not keep the process alive.

followups.q: How do you make a function you wrote cancellable?
followups.a: Accept a `signal` option, call `signal.throwIfAborted()` at safe points, pass the signal down to every API you call, and listen to the `abort` event to clean up resources such as timers or sockets.

followups.q: Does aborting a fetch cancel the work on the remote server?
followups.a: No. It closes the connection on your side. The server may or may not notice; that depends on whether it watches for client disconnect.

followups.q: What is the difference between AbortError and TimeoutError?
followups.a: Most core APIs (timers/promises, fs, events, streams) reject with an `AbortError`. When the signal came from `AbortSignal.timeout`, its reason is a `TimeoutError` DOMException, which you see in `err.cause` or `signal.reason`. `fetch` is different: it rejects with the signal's reason itself, so you get the `TimeoutError` directly. Either way you can tell a timeout from a manual cancel.

mistakes: Using `Promise.race` and assuming the slow operation stopped.
Leaving the race timer running, which delays process exit and leaks timers.
Creating a signal but not passing it down to inner calls.
Expecting abort to interrupt CPU-bound synchronous code.

questions.title: Async iterators, for await, events.once/on
questions.question: What are async iterators and `for await...of`? Where do you use them in Node, and what do `events.once` and `events.on` do?
questions.short: An async iterator is an object whose `next()` returns a promise of `{ value, done }`. `for await...of` calls `next()`, awaits it, and runs the body, one item at a time, so you get natural backpressure. Async generators (`async function*`) are the easy way to create one. In Node, readable streams, `readline`, `fs.promises.opendir`, and `events.on` are async iterable. `events.once(emitter, name)` returns a promise for the next event, and `events.on(emitter, name)` returns an async iterator of events; both reject on an `error` event and accept an AbortSignal.
questions.simple: A normal loop takes items from a full box. `for await` takes items off a conveyor belt and waits when the belt is empty.

explain.p: An object is async iterable if it has a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method that returns an object with `next()`, and optionally `return()` and `throw()`. When you `break`, `return`, or throw out of a `for await` loop, the loop calls `return()` so the source can clean up (close a file, remove listeners).

explain.caption: Lazy pagination: no page is fetched before it is needed.

list: `await once(server, "listening")`: wait for one event; resolves with an array of the event args.
Both reject if the emitter emits `error` while waiting (unless you are waiting for `error` itself).
`for await (const [msg] of on(emitter, "message"))`: each event becomes a loop iteration. Events that arrive while the body is busy are buffered.
Pass `{ signal }` to stop waiting; breaking out of the loop removes the listeners.

explain.note: For processing a stream, `for await` is great for reading. For piping between streams, prefer `stream.pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`, which handles errors and cleanup on both ends.

anim.title: for await over a generator and over events

steps.note: `for await` calls `next()` on the generator and awaits the promise. The generator runs until its own await.
After 10ms the generator yields 1. `next()` resolves with `{ value: 1, done: false }`.
The loop asks for the next value. The generator resumes ONLY now. That is pull-based: the consumer sets the pace.
Second value. Then the generator finishes and `next()` returns `done: true`, ending the loop.
`once` adds a one-time listener and returns a promise. main waits for the event.
The event fires; the promise resolves with the args array, and the listener is removed.
`on` returns an async iterator. Its listener stays attached while we loop.
Two events are emitted synchronously. The first goes to the waiting loop; the second is buffered inside the iterator.
The loop body runs for "hi".
Next iteration takes "bye" from the buffer, then we `break`.
`break` called the iterator's `return()`, which removed the listener. No leak.

followups.q: Is for await over a readable stream fast?
followups.a: It is convenient and handles backpressure, since the stream is only read as fast as the loop consumes. For very hot paths, raw `data` events or pipeline with transforms can be faster, but for most code the difference is small.

followups.q: What happens if the loop body throws while iterating a stream?
followups.a: The loop calls `return()` on the iterator, which destroys the stream, so the file descriptor is released. The error propagates to your code.

followups.q: What is the risk with events.on if the loop body is slow?
followups.a: Events keep arriving and are buffered without limit, so memory can grow. EventEmitters have no built-in backpressure; for real data flows use streams, which do.

mistakes: Using `for await` over an array of already-started promises and thinking it limits concurrency.
Forgetting that `once` resolves with an ARRAY of arguments.
Manually adding listeners in a loop and never removing them (leaks, MaxListenersExceededWarning).
Reading a big file with `readFile` and splitting lines instead of streaming with readline.

questions.title: Error objects, cause, and error types
questions.question: How do you design errors in a Node service? Talk about custom error classes, `error.cause`, stack traces, and operational vs programmer errors.
questions.short: I always throw `Error` objects, never strings, so I get a stack. For known failure cases I create small subclasses like `NotFoundError` or `ValidationError` with a `name`, a stable `code` and maybe an HTTP status, so handlers can branch on them. When I wrap a low-level error I pass `{ cause: err }`, which keeps the original error and its stack. I separate operational errors, expected failures like a timeout or bad input that we handle and report, from programmer errors, bugs like reading a property of undefined, which should be logged loudly and usually crash the process.
questions.simple: A good error is a labelled box: what kind of problem it is, a human message, and inside it the original error that caused it.

list: Branch on `instanceof` or a stable `err.code`, never on `err.message` text.
Node core errors have `code` too: `ENOENT`, `ECONNRESET`, `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`.
`Error.captureStackTrace(this, Fn)` can hide internal frames, but with `class extends Error` the stack is already right.
Return a safe message to clients; log the full error with its cause chain on the server.

explain.p: `new Error(msg, { cause })` (ES2022, Node 16.9+) attaches the original error. `util.inspect` and `console.log` print the cause chain, and loggers like pino serialise it. Before `cause`, people concatenated messages and lost the original stack.

head: Operational
Programmer
rows: Timeout, ECONNREFUSED, 404 from API, invalid user input
TypeError on undefined, wrong argument type, broken invariant
Log, alert, usually crash and restart

explain.note: In the global Express error handler, map known `AppError`s to their status, and treat anything else as a 500 with a generic message. Never leak stack traces to clients in production.

anim.title: Wrapping an error with a cause

steps.note: We call `getUser(7)` inside a try.
The low-level function fails with a plain Error. Its stack points at `dbQuery`.
getUser catches it and throws a domain error, passing the original as `cause`. Nothing is lost.
The caller can branch on the class. A subclass is still an Error.
The custom fields are available to an HTTP error handler.
The original low-level error is still there for logs and debugging.
The stack header shows our name and message, because V8 formats the stack lazily, after the constructor set `name`.

followups.q: Why not throw strings or plain objects?
followups.a: They have no stack trace, `instanceof Error` fails, and many tools (loggers, error trackers) handle them badly. Always throw or reject with an Error instance.

followups.q: Should every error crash the process?
followups.a: No. Operational errors are handled where it makes sense: retry, fallback, or return an error response. Unexpected programmer errors that escape to the top are the ones that should crash and restart.

followups.q: What is AggregateError?
followups.a: An Error that holds several errors in `.errors`. `Promise.any` rejects with it, and you can use it when a batch operation has multiple failures.

mistakes: Matching on `err.message` strings to decide behaviour.
Wrapping errors by concatenating messages and dropping the original stack.
Returning internal error messages and stacks to API clients.
Treating every error the same: either crashing on a 404 or swallowing a TypeError.

questions.title: Retry with exponential backoff
questions.question: Write a retry helper with exponential backoff. Which errors should you retry, and why add jitter?
questions.short: The helper calls the function, and on failure waits `base * 2^attempt` milliseconds, capped at a maximum, then tries again until a max number of attempts, then rethrows the last error. I only retry errors that are likely temporary, like timeouts, `ECONNRESET`, 429 and 503, and only operations that are safe to repeat, meaning idempotent or protected by an idempotency key. I add random jitter so thousands of clients that failed together do not retry together and hammer the recovering service, and I make the waits abortable so retries stop on shutdown or when the overall deadline passes.
questions.simple: If the shop is busy, come back in 1 minute, then 2, then 4. And do not all come back at exactly the same second.

list: Retry: timeouts, connection resets, 429 (respect `Retry-After`), 502/503/504, DB deadlocks or serialisation failures.
Do not retry: 400, 401, 403, 404, validation errors, programmer errors. They will fail again.
Only retry non-idempotent operations (POST payment) if you send an idempotency key so the server can de-duplicate.

explain.p: Without jitter, every client that failed at 12:00:00.000 retries at exactly .100, .300, .700. That creates spikes that can knock over a service just as it recovers (the "thundering herd"). Randomising the wait spreads retries over time.

If three layers each make up to 3 attempts, one user request can become 27 calls to the bottom service. Retry at one layer, set an overall deadline, and consider a circuit breaker that stops calling a service that is clearly down.

explain.note: Log each retry with the attempt number and error code. Silent retries hide real incidents until latency explodes.

anim.title: Backoff: 10ms, then 20ms, then success

steps.note: Start: the service will fail twice, then succeed.
First call fails with a 503.
We have retries left. Delay = 10 * 2^0 = 10ms.
Wait without blocking: other requests keep being served during the sleep.
Second call fails too.
Delay doubles: 10 * 2^1 = 20ms. Each failure gives the service more room to recover.
Third call succeeds.
`return await fn()` hands the value back to the caller. If attempt 3 (the last retry) had failed, line 8 would rethrow the error.
The caller gets a normal result and never knew about the failures.

followups.q: How would you honour a Retry-After header?
followups.a: If the error carries it (seconds or an HTTP date), use that as the delay instead of the computed backoff, still capped by your overall deadline.

followups.q: What is a circuit breaker and how does it relate?
followups.a: It tracks recent failures and, past a threshold, fails calls immediately for a cool-down period instead of retrying. Retries handle short blips; a breaker protects you and the dependency during longer outages.

followups.q: Why `return await fn()` and not `return fn()`?
followups.a: Inside the `try`, only `return await` turns a rejection into a throw that the `catch` sees. With `return fn()` the rejection would skip the retry logic entirely.

mistakes: Retrying every error, including 400s and programmer bugs.
Retrying non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key, creating duplicates.
Fixed delays or no jitter, causing synchronised retry storms.
No cap and no overall deadline, so a request hangs for minutes.

questions.title: Thenables and the microtask cost of await
questions.question: What is a thenable? How many microtask ticks does `await` take for a native promise, a plain value, and a thenable? Is `return await` slower than `return`?
questions.short: A thenable is any object with a `then(resolve, reject)` method; promises adopt thenables, which is how different promise libraries interoperate. Since V8 7.2 (Node 12), `await` on a native promise or a plain value resumes after one microtask tick, because the value is used directly instead of being wrapped. Awaiting a non-native thenable costs extra: one tick for a job that calls its `then`, then one more to resume. Resolving a promise with another promise, like `return somePromise` from an async function, also costs about two extra ticks, so in modern Node `return await p` is actually not slower; it is slightly faster and gives better stack traces.
questions.simple: Awaiting a real promise is one hop through the microtask queue. Awaiting a look-alike object needs an extra hop to ask it for its value first.

explain.p: The Promise spec says: if you resolve a promise with an object that has a callable `then`, the promise does not use the object as its value. Instead it calls `then` (asynchronously, in a microtask) and follows whatever it reports. That is why `await`, `Promise.resolve` and `.then` return values all unwrap thenables.

explain.code:
const thenable = { then(resolve) { setTimeout(() => resolve(42), 10); } };
const v = await thenable;      // 42 after ~10ms

explain.note: Because of this rule, never give a plain data object a `then` method by accident. Returning it from an async function will hang or behave strangely.

head: Expression
Microtask hops before code resumes
Why
rows: PromiseResolve returns the same promise; one reaction job
Wrapped in an already-fulfilled promise, one reaction job
One job calls thenable.then, then one reaction job
return p (in async fn), then caller .then
Resolving with a promise schedules a then-job, then two reactions
One for the await, one for the caller reaction

explain.p: These numbers explain puzzles like "why does this log print after that one". They are rarely a performance concern in real apps; I/O dominates. Do not micro-optimise by removing awaits.

Before V8 7.2, every `await` wrapped the value in a new promise and took 3 ticks. A spec change ("await optimization") let `await` reuse native promises directly, which cut it to 1 tick. It also improved zero-cost async stack traces, which work best when you use `await`, including `return await`.

list: Awaiting a promise subclass or a promise from another library disables the fast path; `PromiseResolve` wraps it and it is treated like a thenable.
Microtasks always run before the event loop moves on, so many awaits in a tight loop can still delay timers and I/O.

anim.title: await null vs await thenable vs a .then chain

steps.note: `a()` runs until `await null`. The value is wrapped in a fulfilled promise; resuming `a` is queued right away (1 tick).
`b()` awaits a thenable. It is not a native promise, so first a job is queued to CALL its `then` method.
A normal chain: the first handler is queued because the promise is already fulfilled.
Synchronous code always finishes first.
Tick 1 of the drain: `a` resumes. One tick for awaiting a plain value.
The job calls `thenable.then(resolve, reject)`. It calls `resolve("T")`, which queues resuming `b`, at the BACK of the queue.
The chain's first handler runs and queues the next one.
`b` finally resumes: two hops for a thenable, so it lands after "tick 1".
The chain continues.
Queue empty. All of this happened before any timer or I/O callback could run.

followups.q: Does `Promise.resolve(nativePromise)` create a new promise?
followups.a: No. If the argument is a native promise with the same constructor, `Promise.resolve` returns it as-is. That is the shortcut the await optimisation relies on.

followups.q: Why is `return somePromise` from an async function slower than `return await`?
followups.a: Returning a promise resolves the function's own promise with another promise, which queues a job to call `then` on it and then a reaction, about two extra ticks. `return await` unwraps it in one tick and then fulfils with a plain value.

followups.q: Can microtasks starve the event loop?
followups.a: Yes. Node drains the whole microtask queue (and nextTick queue) before moving on. A promise chain that keeps queuing more work, or millions of awaits in a sync-looking loop, delays timers and I/O.

mistakes: Saying await always takes 3 ticks (that was before Node 12).
Removing `return await` "for performance"; it is not slower in modern Node and it matters inside try/catch.
Accidentally giving a data object a `then` property.
Thinking `await` yields to timers or I/O; it only yields to the microtask queue until that is empty.
